Ophthalmology · published research

Light-induced eye damage

Selected red or near-infrared treatments reduced photoreceptor injury or improved retinal function in animal and cell models. No direct human clinical benefit is reported.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Selected red or near-infrared treatments reduced photoreceptor injury or improved retinal function in animal and cell models. No direct human clinical benefit is reported.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact light-induced-eye-damage category contains 21 publications, mainly animal and laboratory studies, two fruit-fly reports, one commentary, and mixed-model papers. Rat studies are common; records also include mouse retina, ex-vivo mouse retina, and corneal or retinal cell models. Method tags overlap for papers that combine in-vivo and in-vitro work. No human treatment study was identified. Albarracin et al. 2011

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study in people with light-induced retinal or corneal damage was identified. The source records do not establish prevention of human phototoxic injury, recovery of vision after exposure, or safety for consumer light devices.

Animal evidence

Animal studies use bright-light, white-light, blue-light, oxygen-related, or other retinal injury models. Selected 670 nm and near-infrared protocols report lower photoreceptor loss, reduced inflammatory responses, or improved electrophysiologic function. The direction and size of effects vary with wavelength, dose, timing, and injury severity. Recent fruit-fly experiments report recovery under some red and infrared exposures but not all tested wavelengths; the 950 nm condition did not consistently improve recovery. These distinct models should not be treated as one clinical outcome.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Corneal and retinal cell experiments report blue-light-related DNA or mitochondrial injury and partial protection from red light in selected conditions. An ex-vivo mouse-retina study found neuroprotective changes after blue-light damage. Such preparations omit whole-eye exposure, behavior, and long-term visual function.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols use several red or near-infrared wavelengths, pretreatment or post-injury schedules, and different fluences. Some evaluate repeated exposure over days, while others test a single insult. Dose response is not uniform, and exposure from sunlight, displays, and experimental sources is not equivalent.

Interpretation

Preclinical evidence supports biological activity in selected injury models, but it is not consistent enough to define a protective dose for people. No clinical data in this category demonstrate patient benefit or show that routine light exposure can be made safe by PBM.

Evidence strength in source summaryRetinal protection in animal and cell models: Preliminary Human visual outcomes: No direct evidence
Publications and records21 publications in the exact category.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category is dominated by animal, fruit-fly, retinal-tissue, and cell studies. Selected red or near-infrared protocols mitigate some light-induced injury measures, but wavelength and dose effects vary. No human treatment study establishes prevention or recovery of light-induced eye damage. Injury models do not predict routine human exposure.

Publication and study types

  • The records include rat and mouse models, two fruit-fly experiments, ex-vivo mouse retina, in-vitro cell studies, mixed-model papers, and one commentary.
  • The method labels overlap for mixed studies.
  • No human clinical cohort or patient treatment study is listed; animal cohorts are not deduplicated.
